name: Cold Brew
intro: Cold brew is coffee steeped slowly in cold water, which pulls out sweetness and keeps the sharp, acidic edge to a minimum. It's smooth, mellow and naturally chocolatey. You make it once and enjoy it for days.
heroAlt: Engraved line illustration of cold brew coffee

vessel.name: Tall glass over ice
vessel.note: The batch makes a concentrate. Dilute it to taste when serving.

ingredients.note: Coarse, like breadcrumbs or sea salt. By weight this varies with grind and roast, roughly 80 to 100 g.
Filtered water gives a cleaner taste.

equipment.item: Large jar, pitcher or French press (at least 5 cups)
equipment.alternative: Any clean food-safe container with a lid

equipment.item: Fine mesh strainer plus paper coffee filter or cheesecloth

equipment.alternative: Pre-ground coffee labeled coarse or for French press

steps.title: Grind coarse
steps.body: Grind your coffee coarse, like breadcrumbs. Cold water extracts slowly, so a coarse grind prevents over-extraction and makes it easier to filter later.
steps.tip: Fine grounds make cold brew muddy and bitter.

steps.title: Combine
steps.body: Add 1 cup of grounds to your container, then pour in 4 cups of cold or room-temperature water. Stir gently so all the grounds are wet.
steps.tip: Press down any dry clumps floating on the surface.

steps.title: Steep
steps.body: Cover and steep for 12 to 18 hours. Shorter steeping is lighter and brighter, while longer steeping is stronger and deeper. Room temperature works and is a bit faster, while the fridge is slower and gentler.
steps.tip: If you're not sure, start with 14 to 16 hours in the fridge and adjust next time.

steps.title: Strain
steps.body: Strain through a fine mesh strainer, then a second time through a paper filter or cheesecloth for a clean, sediment-free brew. Be patient, as paper filters drip slowly.
steps.tip: Don't squeeze the grounds, as it can push out bitter flavors and sediment.

steps.title: Store
steps.body: Pour into a clean, sealed container and keep refrigerated. For best flavor, enjoy within about a week.

steps.title: Serve over ice
steps.body: Fill a glass with ice, pour in the cold brew, and taste. This batch is fairly strong, so dilute with water or milk to your liking, often around equal parts.
steps.tip: Start with 1:1 and adjust. Strength varies a lot with beans and steep time.

homeMethods.note: Steep in a French press and plunge to strain. It's easy and needs no extra gear, though the result has a bit more sediment than paper-filtered brew.
A jar with a fine strainer and coffee filter works great and is the most common home setup. The result is clean and smooth.
This is not cold brew. Brew strong coffee, then chill and pour over ice. It tastes brighter and more acidic, and it's ready much faster, but lacks cold brew's smoothness.

tips: This is a concentrate, so dilute to taste.
Use filtered water for a cleaner flavor.
Medium and dark roasts give classic chocolate and nutty flavors, and light roasts can taste fruity but sometimes thin.
Steeping time and strength vary by beans and taste, so adjust.
commonMistakes: Grinding too fine, which causes muddiness and bitterness.
Steeping too long and ending up with woody flavors.
Skipping the second filtration and getting gritty coffee.
Keeping it too long. Freshness fades after about a week.

variations.name: Cold brew with milk
variations.description: Dilute with cold milk and a splash of syrup for a creamy iced coffee.

variations.name: Nitro-style
variations.description: Cafés use nitrogen for a creamy, foamy texture. It's hard to replicate at home without special equipment.

variations.name: Vanilla cold brew
variations.description: Add a splash of vanilla syrup when serving.

history: Cold-water coffee brewing has appeared in various forms around the world, including Japanese slow-drip methods, but the exact origins are unclear and disputed.

seo.title: How to Make Cold Brew Coffee at Home: Smooth and Easy
